opening.headline: The source explains the issue of partial trace collection and sensitive information remaining in attributes, distinguishing it by the roles of collection conditions, context propagation, and detection evaluation.
body: A trace for a single request may be cut off at the service boundary, while the prompt and response remain intact within the same span. These two issues have different root causes.

This lesson examines three layers: OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes, context propagation and data collection conditions, and protection against sensitive information. It then explains a case study on the meaning of span collection settings and identifying reasons why traces may be terminated.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the collection conditions and context propagation of OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes
Roles in sensitive information detection evaluation can be distinguished.

screens.title: Traces are only partial, sensitive information remains unchanged.
screens.lead: We examine two common issues encountered in trace collection. Review the scene to distinguish where each problem arises.

paragraphs: A trace for a single request is interrupted at the service boundary, and only some spans are collected. The gateway's spans and the model service's spans are stored in separate traces, making it impossible to follow a request from start to end.
The properties of the same span include the user prompt and the response body verbatim. Even if names or account numbers are present, they are stored unchanged, with no filtering applied.

The two issues have different causes. If the collection conditions and propagation are misaligned, tracing cannot proceed, and if there is no masking point, sensitive information is stored. One is a measurement issue, and the other is a content issue.
This course explains the conditions for collecting OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes and context propagation, and distinguishes the role of sensitive information detection evaluation.

screens.title: Have you verified whether personal information is being entered into the trace?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: Do you know how far prompts and responses are retained in logs or traces?
items.answer: Many teams are unaware that the body of the document may remain, or only the metadata may remain, depending on the default settings of the measurement library. Knowing the scope of what remains is the starting point for verification.

items.prompt: Have you ever verified that a single request spans a single trace during inter-service calls?
items.answer: The fact that traces are observed across different services does not mean they are connected end-to-end. If a trace ID is generated anew at each boundary, a single request is effectively split into multiple traces. It must be directly verified whether a request appears as a single trace along the call path.

items.prompt: Have you clearly defined whether the sensitive information is protected at the app code, the collector, or the repository?
items.answer: If information is stored in only one location, that layer will retain the lost information. It is safer to implement multiple layers that hide information before collection, retrieve it after collection, and restrict who can view it.

screens.outro: Since the target objects are visible, let's first examine how properties are standardized.

screens.title: OpenTelemetry GenAI Attributes and Span Structure
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: OpenTelemetry standardizes the names and properties of spans, metrics, and events for generative AI operations using the Semantic Agreement (semantic conventions). For example, the span attribute gen_ai.operation.name indicates the type of operation such as "chat" or "execute_tool". Datadog receives traces that adhere to OpenTelemetry's 1.37 above GenAI conventions or the OpenInference conventions. span link expresses relationships that are neither parent-child nor hierarchical, and represents data flow using directional properties such as input and output. The message body can be stored in attributes such as gen_ai.input.messages or gen_ai.output.messages.

terms.tip: In English, this is semantic conventions. It is an agreement that all tools record information with the same name to represent the same meaning.
The span attribute indicating the type of operation. It holds values such as chat or execute_tool.
This is the version requirement for the OpenTelemetry GenAI schema received by Datadog. Attributes from lower versions may not be recognized.
This is a means of expressing a relationship between spans, not a parent-child relationship. It is used for asynchronous operations or batch processing connections.
This is an attribute that can hold the input message body. This attribute represents a typical location where sensitive information may remain.

screens.outro: Having verified the structure of attributes, we will now examine the principle of how traces continue across service boundaries.

screens.title: Collection conditions and context propagation
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to step through and see how the trace progresses when a request moves from service A to B.

steps.title: What is context?
steps.body: Context is an object containing a trace ID and a span ID. Propagation is the mechanism for transferring this context between services. When context is passed between services, the spans from both services belong to the same trace.

steps.title: When A calls B
steps.body: When service A calls service B and the context is carried along in the request, the span created by B becomes a child of the same trace. If the context is not passed along, B starts a new trace. This is exactly why the trace was terminated in the previous case.

steps.title: traceparent header
steps.body: The basic propagator uses the `traceparent` header from W3C TraceContext. This header consists of fields in the order of version, trace ID, parent ID, and flags. All tracing tools must pass this header intact to ensure that tracing does not get interrupted.

steps.title: Who is responsible?
steps.body: Radiation is generally handled transparently by the measurement library. Developers do not need to handle it directly, but tracing is broken in paths that lack a radiation agent. Directly created HTTP clients or message queue paths are typical examples.

steps.title: Collection conditions
steps.body: Collection requires three conditions to be met: the measurement must be enabled, the tracing property must be present, and the API key and endpoint must be correct. If any one of these conditions is mismatched, the span may not arrive or only partially arrive.

steps.title: Check sequence
steps.body: If tracing is interrupted, verify sequentially: whether the header is actually carried in the request, whether the receiving side extracts context from the header and uses it as parent context, and whether both services use the same transport format. This sequence is reused in subsequent examples. As we move from top to bottom, the root cause becomes more specific.

screens.outro: Having understood data collection and dissemination, let's now compare the layers that handle sensitive information.

screens.title: Masking Point and Sensitive Information Detection Assessment
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn about the roles and limitations of the three layers of protection that prevent sensitive information from being exposed.

tabs.label: From the app
tabs.body: In app code, you can modify a span's input and output through a span processor, or you may choose not to export the span itself. This ensures the most robust defense by preventing data from leaving the app. However, direct implementation of the code is required, and any fields that do not conform to rules are passed through unchanged. When new fields are added, the rules must also be updated, requiring proper change management.

tabs.label: Collection then detection
tabs.body: Datadog LLM Observability integrates with the Sensitive Data Scanner to detect personal data, financial information, and medical information within prompt-response pairs. The detection evaluation is performed on both inputs and outputs. This evaluation serves the role of post-incident review—meaning it is designed to identify issues after the fact, not to detect them in real time or during active operation. Therefore, it is essential to understand that this process involves searching for issues after data has already been stored.

tabs.label: View restriction
tabs.body: Data Access Control limits which teams can view data from a specific AI app using the `ml_app` tag. It does not delete the stored information but narrows the scope of people who can access it, thereby reducing exposure risks. Since each app must have a different `ml_app` value to be separated by team, a tag specification must first be established. For example, trace data from a customer service app can be restricted so that only the customer service team and the security team can view it.

tabs.label: Layer combination
tabs.body: The three layers do not replace one another. Defense is composed of three layers: masking before collection, detection after collection, and access restriction. Simply omitting masking within an app because detection evaluation is enabled will result in sensitive information being stored without detection. Likewise, relying solely on access restriction will not prevent exposure within authorized teams. It is easier to design a system where each layer compensates for the risks that the other layers fail to address.

screens.outro: Since we have distinguished the role of each layer, let's examine the meaning of the main text collection settings through an example.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Meaning of the Setting that Disables Prompt Body Collection
screens.lead: When a highlighted section in the following settings is selected, an explanation appears describing what that setting changes. For example, a prompt containing the user's name and account number is retained in the span of a customer service chatbot.

data.text:
client = Anthropic(
    open_telemetry={
        "tracer_provider": provider,
        "traces": {"content_mode": "content"},
    }
)

# content_mode="content" records both prompts and responses.
# The default records only metadata..
# Governance approval must be obtained before changing this value.
# Approval rationale is recorded per application.
# Change history is retained for audit purposes.

marks.note: This value enables content collection. If this setting is present, the prompt containing the user's name and account number remains directly in the span. The scope of collection must be determined based on governance standards, not for development convenience. Since risk levels vary by application, this decision must be made individually for each app, and the person who made the decision along with the rationale must be documented.

When text collection is disabled, the span contains only metadata such as identifier, timestamp, status, and token count. Since sensitive information is not stored, the exposure risk is minimized. The trade-off is that you cannot view input data needed for quality evaluation or reproduction analysis. For apps that absolutely require text, a middle-ground approach is adopted—restricting access to only certain portions and granting view permissions selectively.

This provider determines where to export the span. By attaching a span processor to the export path, you can also implement a method that only hides certain parts of the body. You can hide only the name and account number while preserving the context of the question, enabling both analysis and protection. Regardless of the method chosen, decisions and their rationale are recorded on a per-app basis.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the trade-offs and alternatives for disabling content collection, we will now proceed to cases of trace discontinuation, a different type of issue.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Narrowing Down the Causes of a Trace Break
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the instructor's explanation will be displayed. First, think about what you would like to verify on your own, then try it.

items.prompt: Tracing starts anew at the point where the gateway transitions to a model service. What should we check first?
items.answer: Verify whether the `traceparent` header is actually transmitted with the call request. If the header is absent, the receiving side cannot identify the parent and thus starts a new trace. The header can be directly observed via network captures or gateway logs. If the header is missing, verify whether a proxy is configured on the caller's client. It is common for headers to be lost when they are overwritten with a new object during direct HTTP calls.

items.prompt: If the header is transmitted, what should be verified next?
items.answer: The receiver checks whether the context is extracted from the header and used as the parent. Services that have no measurement enabled or no transceiver configured ignore the header altogether. If the model service runs in a separate runtime, the corresponding measurement library configuration on that side must be separately verified.

items.prompt: Still, if it doesn't continue, where should we look?
items.answer: Verify that both services are using the same propagation format. If one service uses W3C TraceContext while the other uses a different format, they will not be able to recognize each other's headers. In this case, configure one service's propagator or set up the service to handle both formats. After making the changes, verify again that a single request appears as a single trace.

items.prompt: Will turning on sensitive information detection evaluation resolve this issue?
items.answer: No. Detection analysis is unrelated to this issue. Propagation is a measurement issue, while detection is a content issue. Symptoms must be addressed at the correct layer corresponding to their root cause, otherwise time will be wasted. Symptoms where the trace is broken should be handled at the propagation layer, and symptoms where content is lost should be addressed at the masking layer—this is the fundamental principle. Attempting to resolve both symptoms with a single tool often fails to resolve either issue. First, classify the symptoms to determine which layer they belong to.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: What is recorded in traces is determined by governance. GenAI properties are standardized and recorded according to the OpenTelemetry specification, and context propagation links traces across services.

Sensitive information is handled in layers of masking before collection, detection after collection, and reading restrictions. Detection evaluation is a post-hoc review and therefore must be designed in conjunction with the masking at the earlier stage.

Once the initial question is answered, the trace interruption issue is a propagation problem and cannot be resolved by sensitive information detection. Report both the app's risk and the analysis requirements separately for each app.

In practice, there are three key questions to verify: whether tracing continues across service boundaries, whether content is preserved in attributes, and if so, at which layer the preservation is interrupted. If answers to these three questions are available, the trace collection can be described as satisfying both operational and governance requirements. If the verification results do not fully meet expectations, improvements should be prioritized starting with the most critical items.

glossary.def: Records operation types, models, tokens, messages, and other details using standardized span attributes starting with gen_ai.
This is a mechanism that passes trace ID and span ID between services to link them under the same trace.
The propagation headers defined by W3C TraceContext contain version, trace ID, parent ID, and flags.
A post-hoc review and evaluation of detecting and redacting personal information such as privacy data in prompts and responses.
A hook that modifies or filters span data before exporting it from the app.

misconceptions.myth: If detection evaluation is enabled, sensitive information is not stored.
misconceptions.fact: Since this is a post-examination phase, masking and access restrictions must be designed together during the data collection phase.

misconceptions.myth: If tracing is lost, it's a collector's issue.
misconceptions.fact: This is generally a metrics issue due to missing header propagation between services.

misconceptions.myth: Turning off content collection has no impact on analysis.
misconceptions.fact: Since input cannot be viewed, there are limitations for reproduction and quality analysis, so judgment is made on a per-app basis.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: The scope is a governance decision.
GenAI properties are standard specifications and context propagation connects to tracing.
Sensitive information is addressed through layers of masking, detection, and access restriction.
Whether content is collected is determined jointly by the app's risk and the need for analysis.

options: Whether the Sensitive Data Scanner detection evaluation is enabled
Whether the traceparent header carried during a call is used as the parent by the receiving side.
Data Access Control with ml_app tag configuration
checks.explain: If the context propagation between services is interrupted, tracing will not continue. Verify whether the propagation headers are being sent and whether the receiving side is extracting and using them.

wrong.0: Detection evaluation is a content review and is unrelated to trace connections.
wrong.1: Whether the body is collected is determined by the content of span and is unrelated to connection.
wrong.3: View restriction determines who can view it and is unrelated to trace linkage.

checks.intro: You have just learned the order to check the causes of trace termination. First, select what to verify. It is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The first check is whether the header is being passed along and whether the receiving side is using the parent.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This item is not the cause of discontinuity. Consider what needs to be passed between services for tracing to continue.

checks.q: Pair the layers and means of sensitive information defense.
left: Detection of sensitive information in prompt-response pairs after collection
Team-limited access to specific AI app data
Maintain one trace across service boundaries
right: Data Access Control and ml_app tag
checks.explain: The span processor handles collection before, the scanner handles collection after, and Data Access Control manages read restrictions. Traceparent propagation is responsible for trace linkage, not sensitive information.
checks.intro: Pair the defense layers and means. Scores are not recorded.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch here. Please distinguish between what is handled before collection, after collection, viewing restrictions, and dissemination.

When detection evaluation is enabled, broken traces are automatically connected.
Detection evaluation is a function that generates a trace ID.
Detection evaluation fails if tracing is broken.
